headline: Sponsorship pays for youth sports, IMG goes digital, and verification becomes the product.

models.name: Sponsorship-funded youth sports distribution
models.what_it_is: Brands fund youth leagues through the incumbent platform instead of clubs funding themselves: Spectrum's multi-year TeamSnap deal, expanded March 2025, sponsors 720+ leagues through 2027 with jerseys, field signage and custom communications.
models.why_emerging: Club fees keep rising while brands want authenticated local households; the platform that can prove reach to 620,000+ households (per TeamSnap's recent update) can sell that audience and subsidize the sport.
models.technique: Pilot with one brand in a few markets, prove household reach with branded jerseys and signage, then scale to hundreds of leagues; spend sponsor dollars on scholarships, registration relief and equipment so leagues feel the benefit, not just the logo.
models.who: TeamSnap (25M users); Spectrum (partnership since fall 2023, 1,100+ leagues per recent update)
models.for_venture: A verified development record is a sponsor-grade audience: brands will pay to reach club households they can trust, and sponsor dollars could cut family fees — but only once the record itself is trusted.

models.name: Elite academy goes digital, direct to families
models.what_it_is: IMG Academy+ (announced Oct 19) unbundles a 50-year boarding-school development methodology into a consumer app for athletes as young as eight, from $10/month content to live one-on-one coaching and college recruiting help.
models.why_emerging: Families who can't attend a campus will still pay for the brand's development system, and subscriptions turn a one-time camp sale into recurring revenue with national reach.
models.technique: Tier the ladder: cheap on-demand content (1,000+ pieces on habits and leadership) at the bottom, live nutrition and mental-performance coaching with messaging in the middle, recruiting services at the top; sell the methodology, not the facility.
models.who: IMG Academy (CCO Chris Ciaccio); launched Oct 19, 2026
models.for_venture: Don't copy IMG's brand ladder — yours is record first, paid add-ons later — but IMG proves parents already pay monthly for development, not just for registration.

models.name: The AI finance employee for small business
models.what_it_is: BOB is an AI finance employee for small businesses: it keeps the books, sends invoices, accepts payments and holds funds in a deposit account, and owners talk to it over WhatsApp, text, Slack, Teams or email like a bookkeeper.
models.why_emerging: Small operators lose nights and weekends to finance work they hate, and agents can now do it inside the chat tools owners already open — no new dashboard to learn.
models.technique: Meet owners where they already message; bundle bookkeeping, invoicing, payments and a deposit account into one 'employee'; launch in private beta, then use a free agent tier to onboard owners before charging for the money features.
models.who: BOB AI Holdings ($5.5M seed Oct 23, Mischief led, Peter Thiel participating)
models.for_venture: Clubs are small businesses run by volunteers: a chat-first finance agent that chases dues and reconciles payments is your step-3 ops layer, sold to treasurers, not parents.

models.name: Verification infrastructure for agent-written work
models.what_it_is: Blacksmith sells CI cloud built for the agent era: developers now push orders of magnitude more pull requests, and legacy CI can't keep up, so verification — not code generation — is the bottleneck worth paying for.
models.why_emerging: When agents write the code, trust becomes the scarce resource; the layer that turns generated text into something a company will merge is getting repriced upward.
models.technique: Make verification fast and parallel instead of queuing behind generation; sell the merge decision (tests, checks, speed) rather than raw compute; land with engineering teams whose PR volume already broke their old CI.
models.who: Blacksmith ($66M Series C Oct 21, $1B valuation, Sequoia led; 17x ARR, 10,000 companies)
models.for_venture: Every auto-generated rating, schedule or parent report needs a verification pass before families see it — trust is the feature, just as Blacksmith's merge gate is.

models.name: Outcome pricing: cost per workflow, not per seat
models.what_it_is: Enterprise AI buying is shifting from cost per response to cost per business workflow completed correctly, securely and reliably — with planning budgets of $20-50K for a proof of concept and $50-125K for a narrow production workflow.
models.why_emerging: Cheaper models didn't produce cheaper outcomes: a low-cost response that fails, needs rework or breaks compliance costs more than a pricier one that finishes the job.
models.technique: Scope to one measurable workflow with known volume, error tolerance and approval rules; instrument cost per successful completion and error rate; price on completed outcomes and scale only the workflows that prove out.
models.who: Enterprise AI buyers (Gartner Sept 2026 analysis; AWS AgentCore pricing)
models.for_venture: Sell clubs 'a testing day delivered' — kids tested, reports sent, directors briefed — priced per event, not per seat; that turns a one-club pilot into a repeatable sale.

models.name: Machine-to-machine tool marketplace
models.what_it_is: Monid is a marketplace and checkout for AI agents: instead of a developer opening accounts and storing keys with every tool provider, they fund one balance and agents search, compare, call and pay per use across 1,700+ endpoints.
models.why_emerging: If agents start choosing their own tools, discovery, identity, billing and permissions for machine buyers become infrastructure — and humans stop being the checkout step.
models.technique: Aggregate tool providers behind one funded balance; charge provider pricing plus a 10% platform fee with per-call prices in fractions of a cent; win on volume, since the model only works if machine transactions reach enormous scale.
models.who: Monid ($7.7M seed Oct 6, Long Journey Ventures led; 4M+ agent transactions)

signal: Distribution and trust are splitting the market: whoever holds verified households — or verified work — can charge for outcomes instead of seats.
